Barnsley.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Barnsley and South Yorkshire
s1loc: Barnsley anchors its visitor economy on Barnsley Museums, whose Cannon Hall Museum, Park and Gardens at Cawthorne ranks among the most visited free attractions in Yorkshire and the Humber. Experience Barnsley in the grand Town Hall tells the borough story, the Cooper Gallery shows fine art, and Worsbrough Mill keeps a working 17th-century watermill turning, together drawing well over two million visits across the year.

The leisure and activity layer spreads through the surrounding countryside, from the parkland and farm trails at Cannon Hall to the reservoir and woodland walks at Worsbrough Country Park. Locke Park in town offers families open green space and a tower, while the Trans Pennine Trail and the Dearne Valley wetlands draw cyclists, walkers and watersports towards Old Moor and the wider Dearne corridor.

Heritage and culture run deep at Elsecar Heritage Centre, the restored Victorian ironworks village with its Newcomen engine, antique shops and the Elsecar Heritage Railway. Wentworth Castle Gardens and the Stainborough estate sit nearby, and the town centre carries a busy events calendar through The Glass Works, the Mayday Festival and the Barnsley Civic arts venue on Hanson Street.

The visitor trade leans on a growing hotel base around Junction 37 of the M1 and the Tankersley and Dodworth corridors, with a guide scene built on the museums and the Pennine fringe. Barnsley Interchange links rail and coach travel into the Sheffield city region, and the day-trip pull of the Peak District, Cannon Hall and the Dearne Valley feeds a steady seasonal flow.

Darlington.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Darlington and the Tees Valley
s1loc: Darlington trades on being a cradle of the railways, and its visitor economy now centres on Hopetown Darlington, the 35-million-pound attraction opened in 2024 around the old Head of Steam museum. Visitors meet Locomotion No. 1, tour North Road Station Museum and The Stores, and walk the Skerne Bridge of 1825, the oldest railway bridge still in use, with the site expected to draw over 300,000 visits a year.

The leisure and activity layer runs through South Park, the Victorian flagship beside the River Skerne with its lake, aviary and bandstand, and out to the open spaces of the Tees and the surrounding countryside. The Darlington Locomotive Works lets visitors watch the A1 Steam Locomotive Trust build new engines, while family days out reach to nearby Hardwick Park and the wider Tees Valley trails.

Heritage and culture gather around the medieval Market Place, the soaring St Cuthbert's Church known as the Lady of the North, and the landmark Brick Train sculpture by David Mach. The Hippodrome theatre carries touring shows, the Crown Street Library anchors the civic quarter, and an events calendar of markets and festivals keeps the town centre and the historic Pease heritage in view.

The visitor trade draws on a town-centre and out-of-town hotel base and a guide scene built on the railway story, with Darlington station a key stop on the East Coast Main Line and Teesside Airport close by. Frequent rail and road links into Stockton-on-Tees, Durham and Newton Aycliffe, plus the day-trip pull of the Dales and the coast, feed a steady seasonal flow.

Hastings.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Hastings and 1066 Country
s1loc: Hastings built its visitor economy on the seafront and the cliff-girt Old Town, where the ruins of Hastings Castle, raised by William the Conqueror in 1067, look down over the bay. The rebuilt Hastings Pier draws crowds along the front, the West Hill and East Hill cliff railways climb the slopes, and the famous black net shops on The Stade mark the largest beach-launched fishing fleet in Europe.

The leisure and activity layer reaches from the funfair and amusements of the seafront to the wooded valleys of Hastings Country Park along the cliffs towards Fairlight. The Smugglers Adventure in the St Clement's Caves tells the dark side of the coast, Alexandra Park gives families open green space, and watersports, angling and coastal walking keep the bay busy through the summer season.

Heritage and culture cluster on The Stade, where Hastings Contemporary sits among the net huts beside the fishermen's museum and the Jerwood legacy galleries. The medieval lanes of the Old Town, the Shipwreck Museum and the True Crime Museum draw browsers, while the Jack in the Green festival, Hastings Week and the bonfire processions fill the events calendar around the seafront and the town.

The visitor trade leans on a seafront hotel and guest-house base and a guide scene built on the 1066 story shared with Battle Abbey, with tour operators working the cliffs and the fishing quarter. Hastings station links the town by rail to London and along the coast, and the day-trip pull of Rye, Bexhill-on-Sea and the East Sussex coast feeds a strong seasonal flow.

Hartlepool.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Hartlepool and the Tees Valley
s1loc: Hartlepool centres its visitor economy on the National Museum of the Royal Navy at the marina, a re-created Georgian seaport set in the time of Nelson and Trafalgar. At its heart sits HMS Trincomalee, Britain's oldest warship still afloat, built in Bombay in 1817, alongside the paddle steamer Wingfield Castle and the Museum of Hartlepool telling the wider story of the town and its docks.

The leisure and activity layer runs from Hartlepool Marina, one of the most modern in Europe, where powerboating, jet ski experiences and paddle-boarding draw visitors to the water. Seaton Carew offers a broad sandy beach and seafront amusements, Ward Jackson Park gives families open green space, and the coastal path north to the Heugh Headland and the lighthouse keeps walkers busy through the season.

Heritage and culture gather on the historic Headland, where St Hilda's Church crowns the old town and the Heugh Battery Museum recalls the German naval bombardment of 1914. The town carries a busy events calendar, from the Tall Ships legacy at the quay to seafront festivals, while the Borough Hall and the Town Wall mark the deep maritime past of this County Durham port.

The visitor trade leans on a marina and seafront hotel base and a guide scene built on the maritime story and the warship, with operators working the quay and the Headland. Hartlepool station links the town by rail along the Durham coast and into the Tees Valley, and the day-trip pull of Stockton-on-Tees, Billingham and the Durham coast nature reserves feeds a steady seasonal flow.

Birkenhead.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Birkenhead and the Wirral
s1loc: Birkenhead built its visitor draw on the Mersey waterfront at Woodside, where the U-Boat Story displays the sectioned German submarine U-534, raised from the seabed in 1993. The Mersey Ferries cross from the terminal to Liverpool's Pier Head, while Birkenhead Priory, the oldest building on Merseyside, and the historic Cammell Laird shipyard story anchor the town's maritime identity across the estuary.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Birkenhead Park, opened in 1847 as the first publicly funded park in Britain and a model for New York's Central Park, with its boating lakes, Swiss Bridge and grand lodges. Hamilton Square offers one of the finest Georgian set-pieces outside London, and the Wirral coastline and country trails draw families and walkers towards the wider peninsula.

Heritage and culture gather at the Williamson Art Gallery and Museum, purpose-built in 1928, with its celebrated collection of ship models tracing Cammell Laird and the Mersey Ferries. The restored Hamilton Square and the Pacific Road area carry the events calendar, the Wirral Tramway and Transport Museum runs heritage trams, and the town's shipbuilding past frames a year-round programme of exhibitions and tours.

The visitor trade leans on a Wirral hotel base spreading out to Oxton and the coast, with a guide scene built on the waterfront, the park and the maritime heritage. The Mersey ferries and the Wirral rail line link Birkenhead into the Liverpool City Region, and the day-trip pull of Wallasey, New Brighton and the Wirral peninsula feeds a steady seasonal flow.

Bath.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Bath and North East Somerset
s1loc: Bath runs one of the country's great heritage visitor economies, a UNESCO World Heritage city drawing millions of visits a year. The Roman Baths and the Grand Pump Room alone receive over a million visitors annually, while Bath Abbey, the honey-stone Royal Crescent and the Circus give the Georgian city a pulling power matched by few towns of its size in England.

The leisure and activity layer reaches from the modern Thermae Bath Spa, fed by Britain's only natural thermal hot springs, to the green sweep of Royal Victoria Park and the Botanical Gardens below the Crescent. Boat trips and paddling run on the River Avon and the Kennet and Avon Canal, while Alexandra Park and Bath Skyline walks draw families and visitors across the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run deep at the Holburne Museum at the head of Great Pulteney Street, the Jane Austen Centre, the Fashion Museum and the Victoria Art Gallery. Pulteney Bridge and the weir, the Theatre Royal and the Assembly Rooms anchor the events calendar, while the Bath Christmas Market, the Jane Austen Festival and the literature and music seasons fill the city through the year.

The visitor trade leans on a deep hotel base across the Georgian terraces and a busy tour-operator and guide scene built on open-top buses and walking tours. Bath Spa station links the city by rail to London Paddington and Bristol, and the day-trip pull of Stonehenge, the Cotswolds, Wiltshire and the wider West Country feeds a strong year-round and seasonal flow.

Stevenage.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Stevenage and North Hertfordshire
s1loc: Stevenage anchors its visitor draw on Knebworth House just to the south, the turreted Lytton family seat with its Victorian Tudor Revival facade, 28 acres of formal gardens, a maze and a dinosaur trail. Famed for hosting major rock festivals on its parkland, Knebworth pulls big crowds, while Stevenage Museum beneath St Andrew and St George's Church tells the town's Roman roots and pioneering New Town story.

The leisure and activity layer centres on Fairlands Valley Park, 120 acres of parkland once voted among the UK's leading free attractions, with its 11-acre sailing lake. The Sailing Centre runs dinghy, kayak, windsurf and powerboat courses, alongside grass sledging, orienteering and mountain biking, while Stevenage Leisure Park and the surrounding Hertfordshire trails keep families busy through the year.

Heritage and culture gather in the charming Old Town High Street, with its coaching inns and the historic Six Hills Roman burial mounds, set against the bold pedestrianised New Town centre, the first designated under the New Towns Act of 1946. The Gordon Craig Theatre carries touring shows, and a calendar of markets and community festivals keeps both the old and new quarters in view.

The visitor trade leans on a hotel base around the town centre and the A1(M) corridor and a guide scene built on Knebworth, the New Town heritage and the surrounding countryside. Stevenage station sits on the East Coast Main Line with fast links to London King's Cross, and the day-trip pull of Hitchin, Letchworth Garden City and the Hertfordshire towns feeds a steady seasonal flow.
